title: Quantum low-density lattice codes
authors: Timo Hillmann, Jens Eisert, Francesco Arzani
abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes provide a family of promising schemes for encoding discrete quantum information (qudits) into infinite-dimensional bosonic modes based on mathematical lattices. While such codes, when concatenated with discrete-variable codes, are relatively well studied, the construction and decoding of native GKP codes has largely remained open due to the computationally hard problems encountered. To address this challenge, we advocate a strategy of co-designing the decoder and the quantum error-correcting code itself by constructing lattices for which decoding is feasible: The requirement of efficient decoding effectively determines the quantum error-correcting code. This construction is built on classical low-density lattice codes (LDLCs), a lattice analogue of low-density parity-check codes, here lifted to families of GKP codes. Concretely, we introduce quantum versions of classical, randomly constructed LDLCs. We show that after suitable dimensionality reduction these codes have code properties comparable to or better than concatenated GKP-surface codes of equal number of modes. However, the GKP-LDLCs constructed here do not have a strictly sparse parity check matrix, which motivates our study of the performance of natively analog message-passing decoders originally developed for LDLCs when applied to concatenated GKP-LDPC codes. We show that the fully analog, linear-time decoder achieves performances close to state-of-the-art hybrid qubit-analog decoders. To facilitate future research on the structure and performance of general GKP codes, the relevant source code will be released in open-source Julia packages LatticeDecoder.jl and SymplecticGKP.jl.
summary: This paper tackles the difficult problem of decoding native GKP quantum error-correcting codes by co-designing the code structure with its decoder. The authors leverage classical Low-Density Lattice Codes (LDLCs) to build quantum analogues (qLDLCs). They demonstrate that using specialized, fully analog message-passing decoders allows these codes to achieve error correction performance comparable to leading hybrid qubit-analog methods.
main_problem: The primary challenge is constructing and efficiently decoding native Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes, which encode qudits into infinite-dimensional bosonic modes.
main_result: The authors propose a co-design strategy using classical Low-Density Lattice Codes (LDLCs) to construct quantum versions (qLDLCs) whose performance approaches state-of-the-art hybrid decoders.
method: They adapt classical message-passing decoding algorithms, originally developed for LDLCs, to the quantum lattice setting, requiring the co-design of the code structure and the decoder.
model_or_system: The model involves GKP codes, which are bosonic quantum error-correcting codes based on mathematical lattices. The underlying mathematical structure is derived from classical LDLCs.
key_observables: Error rates, code properties (e.g., code distance, logical dimension), and the convergence of message-passing variances.
important_parameters: The dimensionality reduction factor and the convergence parameter $\alpha$ governing the asymptotic behavior of the iterative decoder.
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that efficient decoding requirements can dictate the structure of the quantum error-correcting code, bypassing the direct, hard lattice problems.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the difficulty of native GKP decoding to proposing a co-design strategy based on classical LDLCs, detailing the use of analog message-passing decoders, and finally presenting results showing comparable performance to existing state-of-the-art codes.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses fault-tolerance in bosonic quantum computing platforms, providing a concrete, computationally tractable path forward for implementing high-performance quantum error correction.

The grey dashed line shows the Gaussian with initial mean obtained from the syndrome measurement, and its variance is the channel prior. The red vertical dashed lines show the decoded lattice point obtained after the hard decision, see Eq. (4). For visualization purposes, Gaussians are not normalized.
